Morire typeface

Harriet Goren’s sketchy, vibrating typeface, drawn over one weekend in an experimental type workshop and soon used throughout Ray Gun.

Source
Sharan Shetty, “The Rise And Fall Of Grunge Typography”, The Awl (2012), archived copy
Creator
Harriet Goren
Made
1993 or 1994 (Goren, quoted in The Awl)
Style
Grunge typography (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Intuitive, angsty, raw
Evidence
Based on The Awl’s interview with Goren. The only image found, The Awl’s sample, is 600 × 103 px, too small to describe the letterforms. T-26 stopped selling the font in 2004, so no current specimen was found.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Goren told The Awl she designed the whole typeface over one weekend in 1993 or 1994, in an experimental typography course taught by P. Scott Makela at the Center for Creative Imaging in Camden, Maine. The Awl.

Makela suggested she send it to David Carson; a few months later she found Morire “emblazoned all over the pages” of Ray Gun, credited and used on a cover. The Awl.

The Awl says the design was inspired by Monteverdi’s song “Sì ch’io vorrei morire” and is “all sketch and shadows, as though the letters are in perpetual and subtle vibration”. The Awl.

T-26 distributed Morire and stopped in 2004. Wikipedia, citing The Awl, lists Morire with Hat Nguyen’s Droplet and Eric Lin’s Tema Cantante as “signature grunge fonts”. The Awl; Wikipedia.

Why it belongs

Morire shows how the style spread: a quickly made, deliberately rough font moved from a workshop to Ray Gun to a commercial foundry within months.

Borrow

Draw display letters as clusters of loose sketch lines, so that their edges seem to vibrate.

What to review next

  • Find a specimen or Ray Gun page that shows Morire at 800 px or more, and record the issue that used it on the cover.
